speakeroldname: Hon. R. J. MANION (Minister of Railways and Canals):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in view of
the fact that during the two weeks this debate has been going on, two out of three speeches have been coming from the other side of the house, and that on three occasions at least this side of the house permitted hon. gentlemen opposite to exceed their time against the rules of the house, I must confess that, after extending this courtesy to hon. gentlemen opposite, I am somewhat surprised by the attitude now' taken by the chief whip of the Liberal party in trying to prevent me from speaking.
In speaking for the forty minutes at my disposal in closing the debate on the second reading of this bill, I do so with mingled feelings because, in moving the second reading nearly two weeks ago, I particularly requested of all sides of the house that, as far as possible, they should deal with the question on a high plane. I will quote my words:
I sincerely hope that when this bill goes to the committee of the -whole or is otherwise disposed of by this house it will be dealt with on exactly the same high plane, because I submit that this is no time for party strife, and I do not believe that the people of this country in these critical times, particularly having in mind the incidents of last week, are looking for party strife on a matter which is so serious to them as is this question.
I repeated the same suggestion later in my remarks. I endeavoured at that time to take a non-partisan, non-eontrove-rsial and unbiased attitude on this whole question, and this is proved by the commendations which I have received from the other side of the house from various speakers, on the high stand taken at the opening of the debate; though their commendations have made me sometimes wonder if I was not wrong. Then the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) took exactly the same attitude as I did. He took an unbiased, non-partisan attitude, certainly one which supported the position which I had taken. He was followed later by the hon. member for North Bruce (Mr. Malcolm) later by the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Yeniot), this afternoon by the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power), by the hon. member for West Edmonton (Mr. Stewart),
IMr. Speaker.]
and various others who took exactly the same broad attitude towards this very important question. I may add that a number of speakers on the other side of the house who belong to the third party took the same position. Of course they differed in regard to details of the bill, but on the whole they took a non-political stand, although they were critical of some portions of the bill. I congratulate them and the others I have mentioned on their very fair stand.
Speaking after me, the hon. member for North Waterloo obviously spoke on behalf of the whole Liberal party. He was their spokesman for the time being, and I must confess that sometimes since the beginning of this debate I have found myself wondering how he felt, after having stood up in this house and showing a very fair-minded attitude and more or less pledging the party, to see a large portion of the party desert him. That is not his fault, and I am not urging it as any criticism against him; yet I found myself wondering over and over again, as I listened to the change in tone after the hon. member for North Waterloo and one or two others had spoken, as to what caused that complete change of attitude voiced by so many hon. gentlemen who followed a little later in the debate.
.Somie hon. MEMBERS:	The Prime Minister's speech.

The attitude of hon. members had changed long before the Prime Minister's speech. However, I will deal with that later. Criticism did come, it is true, in regard to some details of the bill, from this side of the house. I admit that. I find myself again wondering if it was not a fact that the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) came to the conclusion there must be some difficulty in our party, and therefore decided he would do well to take advantage of it and perhaps split the party on a vote. However, I am just guessing as to that.
I do say this, that I listened to every speech made in this debate from all sides of the house, and I heard no speech from this side-and in that I include the Prime Minister's speech-I heard no speech from this side of the house which was really partisan in any way. I shall try to establish that as I go along. But some hon. members on the other side, at least half of them, made political speeches. They found fault not only with the bill-and I do not quarrel with that -but they imputed motives to us. The right hon. gentleman who leads the opposition

C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill-Mr. Manion
spoke of sinister designs behind this bill. I doubt if anybody could have used more severe language than to suggest that there was anything in the shape of a sinister design behind this bill. It is true hon. members opposite-as they did also a minute ago-in their speeches did charge the Prime Minister with having taken a partisan attitude. I deny it. He followed the hon. member for West Lambton (Mr. Gray) whose speech was a very very severe castigation, from a political standpoint, of everything coming from this side of the house. He followed the speech of the right hon. leader of the opposition who moved an amendment which could not possibly be accepted, the right hon. gentleman who used the expressions I have just quoted.
The right hon. gentleman opposite suggested sinister motives, and so that there may be no mistake I shall read his words as they are reported in Hansard. At page 2853 of Hansard the right hon. gentleman is reported as follows:
But if that cannot be done,

That is, if the amendment cannot be accepted-
-I must confess that so far as I personally am concerned I should not find it possible to support the second reading of this bill, because I would find in the refusal by the government of a declaration of this kind, evidence that there must be a sinister design which is not apparent on the face of the measure itself.
What possible suggestion could anyone make of a more partisan nature than that the whole government of my right hon. leader had a sinister design behind the bill? I say the leader of the government was justified in becoming a bit irritated by the speech of the leader of the opposition, and1 even more so by the speech of the hon. member for West Lambton.

My remark
was conditioned upon the acceptance of the amendment.

Upon the acceptance of
an amendment which could not be accepted, because it amounted practically to a six months' hoist, an amendment which the Speaker himself ruled out of order. Yet we were asked by the right hon. gentleman to accept the amendment; in the event of not accepting it he suggested there was a sinister design behind the bill.
It is true the Prime Minister did quote Sir Wilfrid Laurier as having said that the National Transcontinental and the Grand Trunk Pacific would cost the people some $13,000,060 when the cost was hundreds of millions. However that is a matter of history.
There was nothing wrong with the quotation; it was absolutely according to facts. He also pointed out that Mr. Blair, the Minister of Railways of Sir Wilfrid Laurier's day, had resigned because he did not agree with the proposal to build the Transcontinental railway. However those are historical facts.
I do not remember any statement made by the Prime Minister which was of a partisan nature.
Oh, oh.

On the other hand, the
hon. member who has just said something to me which I did not hear, the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie) got up to-day in this House of Commons and commended me upon my moderation, and hoped that I would show the same type of moderation in my speech to-night. But here is the way he showed moderation: I marked down two or three headings as the hon. member spoke. He talked of an iniquitous bill; he talked about an insidious measure; of the Machiavellian hand of this government; of a Tory triumvirate; of a Tory conspiracy. I found myself again asking the question:	If
that is a moderate speech, what would he say if he were immoderate?
The right hon. leader of the opposition, in his speech, of course dealt with the bill in most moderate fashion. I shall give some of the statements he made. He said the bill was sinister in design. He said it would deprive parliament of its fundamental rights; that it would adversely affect the Intercolonial railway and the rights of the maritime provinces. I ask hon. members just to note the geographical distribution of his phrases. He said it might result in the shut-down of the Hudson Bay railway project-he had jumped from the maritimes to the Hudson bay. He said the limitation of the board of trustees was unfair to organized labour; that was a touch for labour. He said that the powers granted the trustees "may effectively bring about amalgamation," as to which, unlike certain of his followers, he was "unalterably opposed." I say that the attitude of the right hon. leader of the opposition was merely a camouflage, that he was merely pretending to take a moderate attitude in connection with the bill, that he was simply carrying out the usual policy of an opposition whose duty it is to oppose. He is opposing the measure.
I do not wish further to deal with that line of thought, but may return to these matters later. In the remaining time at my disposal I shall turn my thoughts to the charges made by some hon. members.

C.N R,-C.P.R. Bill-Mr. Manion
The hon. member for West Lambton made a very partisan speech. He made the statement that the position of president and chairman being divided under this bill would have a very serious effect on the national railway.
No, no.
He opposed very strongly the division of this power. I simply point out-
I do not wish to interrupt the minister, but I commended the minister on the very fact that there should be this dissociation.

I accept the hon. member's correction. However, some hon. members made that statement. Some suggested the arrangement would be detrimental to the railways. I have a list of sixteen American railroads on which such an arrangement obtains. The hon. member for West Lambton said that the government was seeking to foist its trustees on the country, and keep them in that position. He took that stand. I cannot agree with him because if the government had desired to do that it would have gone a whole lot further in carrying out the recommendations of the royal commisssion in that regard. At page 64 of the report it is recommended by the commissioners how the trustees shall be appointed in case of a vacancy. It is stated in the first sentence at page 64:
Vacancies among the trustees shall be filled from a panel of eight named by the remaining trustees.
But when the bill was going through the Senate it was changed so that the panel would be supplied not by the remaining trustees but by the remaining trustees with the addition of the chairman of the Board of Railway Commissioners and President of the Exchequer Court of Canada-in other words widening the base. If we had been desirous of perpetuating our trustees we would not have widened the base for the framing of the panel, because it will be remembered that the president of the exchequer court, for whom I have the greatest respect, was an outstanding Liberal, and a minister in a former Liberal government.
Another of the complaints, this one I think from my hon. friend the member for West Lambton, was that this bill by clause 16 would lead to amalgamation. Of course laws can be broken, but this measure is not being enacted for the purpose of permitting amalgamation. I think it was Daniel O'Connell who at one time said he could drive a coach and four through any act of parliament, and this act may be like others in that respect. But my right hon. leader, the Prime Minister, gave the pledge that I had already mentioned-that
[Mr. Manioa.J
we do not intend this bill to bring about amalgamation, and we have given the pledge that an amendment will be moved to protect against that possibility. It would be also a breach of trust on the part of the trustees appointed to look after the welfare of the Canadian National Railways should they take it upon themselves to adopt any such policy, and I do not think this or any government would consider appointing to such an important position men who would do this.
Then it was suggested that this measure is for the purpose of wrepking the Canadian National Railways. I say, and have said on many other occasions, that any man who would set out intentionally to wreck the Canadian National Railways would not be fit to bear the name Canadian or to represent any constituency in this house. Canada has too much interest in, is too much bound up with, the Canadian National Railways; that great transportation system is too intimately related to our national life, for anyone on either side of the house to endeavour to wreck it.
The hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Beaubien) claimed, as did the hon. member for Cartier (Mr. Jacobs), that this bill could only mean amalgamation, and the hon. member for Provencher opposed it for that reason. If that is the object in view, why is the bill so strenuously opposed by the Canadian Pacific Railway? That, I think, is a sufficient answer, for Mr. Beatty has taken the position throughout the country that he believes amalgamation is the proper solution of Canada's railway problem, yet the Canadian Pacific is opposing this bill very strongly,-they did so in the Senate, and they are not favourable to it at the present time.
The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Heenan)-I am sorry I do not see him here at present-spoke of the decrease in wages to be brought about, and said that already there had been a decrease on the Canadian National, as I understood him, of $125,000,000 from 1929 to 1932. I find there has been an actual decrease of $59,000,000, a little less than half the amount the hon. gentleman gave, but as the hon. gentleman is so often not more than half right I suppose this is in line with his usual accuracy in such matters. He also took the attitude that this measure was going to injure labour, and asked for consideration of what he called the human element in industry. Of course we must all think of the human element-and if I may be permitted to refer to my own constituency, it is, I think, more a labour constituency than that of the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River-I am just as anxious for the welfare of the industrial class, the working class so-

C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill-Mr. Manion
called, as any one in this house, and I do not except the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River although I do not speak so often about it as he does. I even go so far as to admit that our economic system is at a fault in permitting conditions to exist that have existed in this depression and other depressions in the past, and that we will have to correct those conditions so that men thrown out of work in any industry will have some care given them. I admit that, but at the moment such measures have not been put into effect and cannot be put into effect under the conditions existing at this time. During all the years that the hon. gentleman administered the Department of Labour in the late government I did not notice that he put any such policies into effect.
But I do not think it is proper in this house to argue the question from the standpoint of any one class in the community. It seems to me that an hon. member represents every class not only in his own constituency but in all the country; at least that is the position I have taken as a member of parliament. And while the argument may be made that there should have been a representative of the railway workers on the commission or the board of trustees, what about the agricultural workers? We have in this country under 200,000 railway workers and over 1,000,000 agricultural workers, and one class is just as dependent on the railway as the other, because the agricultural people cannot buy anything that they require to eat or wear or use that does not pay toll to the railways. So if 200,000 or less railway workers must be represented surely the agricultural class have the same right.
My friend the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth), together with the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speakman), the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Kennedy), the hon. member for Wetaski-win (Mr. Irvine), the hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail) and others, took what I consider a fair attitude; but I wish to refer to one statement made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. He said the bonds of the railway should be exchanged for stocks. If the holders were willing, yes, I agree. But you cannot take possession of the bonds and give stock on which dividends would be paid only when earned, unless you are prepared to repudiate the country's pledge, because the bonds of the Canadian National Railways are guaranteed by this government, and unless we come to the point, which we have not reached yet, that we repudiate our obligations, we cannot force the holders of these bonds to exchange them for stocks.
The hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) complained that there was no labour representative on the commission. I point out that there was no class representation of any kind on the commission. Perhaps I was a little unfortunate in saying that Lord Ashfield and Mr. Loree represented bondholders and stockholders in Great Britain and the United States. I did not mean that they were chosen for that purpose; I simply meant to point out that as there were hundreds of millions of dollars of Canadian Pacific securities held in Great Britain and Canadian National bonds in the United States, it was the opinion of the government that it would bring about a better understanding if we had on the commission a representative from each of these great countries. I think that was a reasonable and logical attitude to take. But, as pointed out this afternoon by some speaker, labour was considered in this report. Section 190 deals with contractual relations of labour, and a clause was put in the bill by Senator Murdock to protect labour in changes brought about by cooperation, so that the labour people on the two great systems would get a fair deal. Throughout the hearings before the commission and also before the Senate committee representatives of many different labour organizations appeared and made representations, so that labour did have opportunity to put its case before both the commission and the Senate committee.

A number of different speakers, particularly the hon. member for Toronto West Centre (Mr. Factor) and the hon. member for Shel-bume-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston), stated that when the Canadian National Railways in 1923 went through the process of reorganization or coordination, or whatever the term was, they had been taken over in a dilapidated condition, and it was pointed out what wonderful work was done in coordinating these straggling nonentities into one system.
Hear, hear.

Let me quote the words of the hon. member for Toronto West Centre. He spoke of the responsibility-listen to this; it is rather good:
The responsibility of joining disjointed, disconnected, dilapidated, insolvent and bankrupt lines of railways into one national system.
I thought this was rather effective from his own standpoint, and I found myself thinking of a remark made by a great gentleman of his own race about fifty years before he was born, Disraeli, who became prominent as a prime minister of England, who on one occasion spoke of Gladstone as being "intoxicated with the exuberance of his own verbosity." I wonder if my hon. friend had not been a bit carried away by his own verbosity. Let me give some of the facts very briefly. In the first place the Intercolonial was then and is now a high-class railway. I do not think it is any better railway now than it was in the old days. The Grand Trunk railway was built in the fifties and was and has been throughout all these years one of our greatest railways running from Portland on the east through the southern part of Canada to Chicago on the west. The Transcontinental

and the Grand Trunk Pacific have the finest roadbeds ever built in this dominion and the lowest grades through the mountains. In addition to that there was the Canadian Northern, which I have left to the last because there may be some criticism of it; but even that w'as not in anything like the condition my hon. friends painted. To prove I am not altogether wrong in my statement, I might as well quote one whom my hon. friends opposite always accept, and that is Sir Henry Thornton, who, to the regret of all of us, died recently. In the 1922 report of the Canadian National Railways signed by him, he made a few statements about the condition of the road, and I shall put them on record just for the sake of future discussion. He said:
1922 completes the four-year period of unified management of the former Canadian Government Railways and the Canadian Northern railway system.
Then he says:
During the period the government has provided large sums of money for the physical improvement of these properties, for coordination facilities, for additional rolling stock and for branch line construction.
Then a little lower down:
While the demands for capital expenditure on a system of such extent in a growing country, as the former board stated, are never ending, yett it may now be said that the three groups of lines, until recently the Canadian National Railways, enter the consolidation in excellent physical condition and operating at a high mark of efficiency as regards actual performance or movement of traffic and other factors controllable by management. When we suggested cutting down the salaries which were being paid to some of the officers of the system, salaries of very large proportions in times like these, for which the people of Canada had to dig down in their pockets and pay by way of taxation, we took the attitude with the late management, as we have taken it with the present management, that irrespective of whether or not these officers were really earning these salaries running up to $30,000 and $50,000 and $60,000, they were too high to be paid under present conditions. It is only beginning its career; its greatness is only starting. This country can go forward with an optimistic attitude concerning its future, and I believe that in enacting this legislation into law we shall be laying the foundation which will make both the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific greater roads than they have ever been in the past.

Hon. W. A. GORDON (Minister of Immigration and Colonization) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to amend the Soldier Settlement Act to provide for the remission of interest in certain cases and the application of payments made to reduction of principal indebtedness; and for additional credit on payment of arrears or instalments; the removal of the lien on the equipment of soldier settlers; and for the application of certain of these provisions to British family settlers by consent of the British government.
Explain.

I wonder if the minister
would be good enough to explain.

Perhaps I could explain
it better in committee, but if hon. gentlemen would like the explanation now I can give it. The bill to be founded upon this resolution is remedial in its character with respect to soldier settlers and others owning land or under contract to purchase land the title to which is at present in the crown.
The first part of the resolution refers to the remission of interest. In the bill founded upon the resolution it will be proposed to remit the interest accruing for the twelve months immediately preceding the standard date as determined and interpreted by the statute. In order to avoid the error that arose in connection with the thirty per cent reduction, for the sake of those who have paid their interest it is proposed that credit be given in such cases by a reduction of the principal indebtedness.
The remainder of the resolution has to do with extending credit, dollar for dollar, for the years ending with the standard dates in 1927 to those who pay the whole or part of the instalments falling due during those years.

Hon. members will remember that in 1930 the interest was spread, so this bill will deal from the period from 1932 to 1937.
Will the minister say a word about the British settlers?

I presume the hon. member for Comox-Alberni has reference to what is known as the three thousand family scheme. The bill founded upon the resolution will make reference to the situation of those settlers and will indicate the couree to be followed by the government in the event of the agreement under wdiich these settlers came to Canada being changed, which of course would have to be with the consent of the British government. It is contemplated that appropriate representations will be made in order to secure that end.

Will there be anything in the
bill to take care of those soldiers w7ho have purchased under the soldier settlement board during the last six or seven years, and who do not come under the original act?

I would remind hon. members that the house is not in committee.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Baker in the chair.

I should like to ask the minister if he can answer the question I just asked, whether it is intended to do anything for those soldiers who have purchased land during the last seven or eight years, and who do not come under the original scheme. There are many returned men, as the minister knows, who have purchased land under the soldier settlement board and who are in great difficulties.
Those cases will be provided for in the legislation.
What is implied in the words "the remission of interest in certain cases"?
I was going to ask the same question. Is this to be a general act covering all cases or is it to cover only certain cases?
The act will provide for the remission of interest charges which accrue during the twelve months immediately preceding the standard date in 1932.
For every soldier settler?

Yes, with the exception of persons falling under the agreement between

Soldier Settlement Act
His Majesty's Secretary of State for the Dominions and the government of Canada, which has reference to the three thousand family scheme. As I indicated a moment ago, the legislation founded upon the resolution will show the course the government will follow with respect to these settlers. The matter will be taken up with the British government in order to obtain their consent to the application of these remedial measures to the settlers, and to have the cost apportioned as the agreement contemplates in other cases.

What I had in mind was whether this was to be a general act covering all settlers or whether it was to be discretional, to apply only in certain cases. I understand, however, that it is a general remission.
Yes.

Can the minister give us the number of settlers under the three thousand family scheme who have returned to the old country? I should like to know what percentage made good in Canada and what percentage returned to England.

I am afraid I have not those figures, but I believe such an analysis could be made. In all probability I could have that done by the time the item in the estimates comes up for consideration, and I will give the information at that time, unless it is necessary that the hon. member have it now.

I cannot understand where there is any advantage in introducing legislation in this roundabout way whereby we are forced to discuss a resolution couched in very vague terms instead of having a bill before us which we could discuss intelligently. Presumably there must be some purpose in bringing in legislation in this vague way and presumably there is some sort of a mantle of secrecy over the legislation until it is discussed in committee. This is the sixteenth of the month and under date of the tenth this was all published in the British Columbia papers at far greater length than the minister is giving it to-night. Does the minister think that that is a desirable custom to have in effect?
I do not read the British Columbia papers.
Shame!

I have not had an opportunity to see what they said about the legislation. There is one thing certain, they never got their information from me. Sometimes 53719-196J
the newspapers are good guessers but I can assure the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) that I have not followed any circuitous route in bringing this resolution before the committee. The subject matter of this resolution has been given very earnest study by those charged with the administration of the act, and it is hoped that it will meet with general approval among the settlers. There is nothing further from my mind than to cloud this matter in mystery, as is suggested. I really cannot understand where the newspapers got their information.

The resolution is essentially vaguely worded as compared with the definite language which would be used in a bill. I am not complaining of that, I simply say that presumably there must be some useful purpose to be served by this method. Why was this information given out to the British Columbia newspapers to a fuller extent than we have had it to-night? The papers published this information on the tenth, but it would have to come from Ottawa, so it must have been given out before that date. I suggest that there must have been a leak somewhere. I am not blaming the minister but I do contend that the information published could not have been based on a guess because it was a very definite statement. If the minister is satisfied I do not suppose I need worry, but it does not seem to be a desirable thing to have information leak out through the press before it is given to the House of Commons.

Quite a number of soldier settlers are not residing upon the land which they took up under the act but still have an equity therein. I should like to know if any easement is being provided by this bill to take care of such cases.

I imagine that would be purely a question of adjustment between the soldier settler who had sold the land and the soldier settler who was on the land. The debtor to the government would be the settler now upon the land.

That hardly answers my question. The situation in the west is that many of the men on the land have not been able to make their payments to the soldier settlement board. The soldier settler who has an equity in a piece of land sees that equity gradually vanishing. I have one case in mind where a soldier settler has an equity of $2,000 in land that has been sold to another party under the tripartite agreement. The purchaser
Soldier Settlement Act

of that land has not been able to make his payments to the board and interest is accruing. The soldier settler is not actually upon the land and I want to know if he will be taken care of by this legislation.

This legislation will remit the interest accruing in 1932 under the contract. So far as the board is concerned the equity will be paid to the original settler as soon as the tripartite settler completes his contract.

Could the minister give the committee an idea of the amount of accrued interest now due and the amount proposed to be remitted under this bill? Is it proposed to remit all interest that has accrued or, if not, what part?

It is proposed to remit all the interest for the twelve months immediately preceding the standard date in 1932. Hon. members will remember that there is a standard date for both western Canada and eastern Canada. For the twelve months prior to the standard date in 1932 the interest will be remitted to all those who have not paid. Those who have paid interest during 1932 will be placed in equation with those who have not paid by having an appropriate amount credited upon their contracts.
That is upon the principal?

Any payment made after this year and until the standard dates in 1937 will be credited at the rate of two dollars for every dollar paid. As hon. members will recall, these payments are amortized and it does not matter whether it is interest or principal, they will get credit no matter what they pay.
Are they charged interest upon the past due amortized payments?
That is interest upon interest?
Yes.
I am not sure of that point.

Would they get dollar for dollar on that?
[Mr. Bothwell.l
They will get dollar for dollar on anything they pay during those years.

What is the standard
date for western Canada?

October 1 for western
Canada, and November 1 for the provinces lying east of Manitoba.
Do I understand that the remittance of interest for 1932 will date back twelve months from that standard date? What about the principal that is owing?

If the hon. member will
recollect, the interest is joined to the principal, if I may put the matter in that way. As regards anyone indebted under contracts or agreements made prior to January 1, 1933 if payments are made in respect of arrears, or of any instalment due up to and including the standard date in 1936, the soldier settler will be credited with double the amount of the payment.

There are quite a number of soldier settlers not only in the riding of North Battleford, but clear across northwestern Canada. May I ask the minister if he understands the objective to which the different locals of the soldier settlers in these different areas are directing their efforts?

Who is the head of the
organization?
There are different locals and a head to each one. I do not think there is any official head of them all. There is a president and a secretary for every local.
Does my hon. friend refer to the soldier settlement unions?
Yes.

Their propositions were
received by the director.

That is the point to
which I am coming. I understand the department over which the minister presides was endeavouring to find out the minimum objective of these soldier settler unions that have been organized right across western Canada for a set purpose, that is to try to find out how they could reasonably remain on the land. In organizing themselves towards this end and in coming to definite conclusions in regard to how they could remain on the land, they worked out one or two main objectives. One was that if they were going to remain there under existing conditions of low prices with farms bought at inflated values

Soldier Settlement Act
and with large sums of principal and interest owing, there would have to be either a total cancellation or a fair adjustment of interest from 1929. If I understand correctly the attitude of the soldier settler unions, they want no interest charges added from 1929 and in their opinion any interest paid between 1929 and 1933 ought to be allowed on the principal, but they definitely state that no interest should be added to the principal accruing from 1930 on, that is from the last revaluation of the soldier settlers' lands. If the department is allowing only a rebate of interest for a year, this is not meeting the viewpoint of the soldier settler unions, and I do not think the legislation will go far enough. I thought it of importance to bring this point before the minister at this time in order to see if he could not try to meet the desires of these men who served their country at such small cost to us, who were overseas for years fighting the battles of Canada, who then came back, bought land at distorted values and are now up against a serious proposition in endeavouring to hold land which they desire to retain and to hand on to their dependents.

What the hon. member
has just said has of course been under my review and from the facts that I have been able to gather, perhaps the hon. member is seeking for the soldier settlers more even than they want themselves. I was well aware that Mr. Price, the gentleman to whom reference has been made, was president of the soldier settlers' union, and on behalf of a very large body of soldier settlers on the land representations have been made by the unions from time to time to the department. Those representations have all been taken into consideration and a number of conferences have been held throughout not only western but eastern Canada making a general review of the situation in the light of present conditions as well as in the light of the situation in which the soldiers .generally find themselves. When I say that the hon. member asks more than the soldier settlers union itself asks, probably he would not urge the proposition he has just outlined. In order to make the position clear, may I read a letter which I received from Mr. Price, president of one of the unions, under date of February 14, 1933.

May I ask what is
Mr. Price's local?
The hon. gentleman knows who he is. He is Mr. H. J. Price, the man to whom I referred a moment ago.

I am not clear as to
his district.

He is president of the
soldier settler union and the letter is dated from Saskatoon.
Union of Saskatchewan?

Yes. It reads:
Dear Mr. Gordon:
I have spent the day discussing with Mr. Maglad'ery, General Ross-
That is Judge Ross, I believe, of Yorkton, Saskatchewan, who is very deeply interested in the welfare of the soldier settlers and the soldiers generally.
-soldier settlers, and representatives of the board, the problems of the settlers and, as a result, we submitted certain conclusions for your consideration. The submissions are generally satisfactory to the delegates who have attended the conference to-day, and I believe will meet the situation.
If you can see your way clear to implement these recommendations by legislation, I will undertake to recommend to the soldier settlers' unions that, barring any unforeseen calamity not at present within our contemplation, the unions should refrain from making any further representations on matters of policy in connection with soldier settlers during the currency of the arrangements which are now recommended to you. I have no doubt that the soldier settlers' unions will accept my recommendation in this regard.
Yours faithfully,
H. J. Price,
President, Soldier Settlers' Union.
The recommendations that Mr. Price has reference to in that letter are incorporated in the legislation that will be founded upon this resolution.
The union refers apparently to Saskatchewan.
I believe it includes some parts of Alberta.

In the district that I represent there is a settlers' association of that nature and they keipt aloof from that union because they were not satisfied with the proposals put forward by it. Not anticipating that this matter was coming up to-night, I have not my papers with me, but my recollection is very definite that they went on record they would be satisfied with nothing less than a total remission of past interest, that is, I presume, since the date of the last adjustment of 1930. They said that it was no use beating about the bush or pretending to be able to pay something they could not pay, and conditions were such that they were reluctantly compelled, not perhaps to demand, because we do not demand from the government, but to submit that the only acceptable
Soldier Settlement Act

arrangement, acceptable because there was a possibility of its being carried out, would be a total remission of interest. I have a very definite request from them to that effect. The minister says, and says truly, that these payments are all by way of amortization. A man does not owe $100 and pay 8 per cent interest; he pays a sum capitalized or amortized over twenty-five or thirty years. The minister says that he is going to rebate the interest. Will it not be a very complicated thing to arrive at the interest for any specific year? How is the settler to know to what rebate he is going to be entitled?

I am told that there will
be no difficulty in identifying the interest for 1932, because that is separated in the ledgers. With respect to the following years, the act makes provision for a credit of one additional dollar if one dollar is paid. If he pays one dollar, he gets credit for two. It is putting a premium on thrift rather than otherwise.

The minister has made it clear that there is to be a remission of interest from 1932, and the resolution says, "and the application of payments made to reduction of principal indebtedness." Is that payments of interest made? I presume it would be, because it is all in the one sentence.

If the 1932 interest was
paid by any settler, then in order to bring his position to an equality with those who did not pay but whose interest was remitted, the payment of those who did pay is credited upon their payments falling due.

When the
interest is credited, does the man also get an additional one dollar credit?
No. For the one class the interest is remitted because it was not paid for 1932. As regards the other class who paid the interest, the person under the contract gets credit on his payments generally.
Just to the amount of the interest?
For that year.

To the
amount of the interest only?
For that year.

The additional credit on payment of arrears or instalments of arrears-that is the dollar added to the dollar-applies in the future and only on principal payments? Is that correct, or does it apply also to interest?
It applies to both interest and principal payments.
To all payments?

To payments made from
March 31, 1933 to March 31, 1936. Wherever a payment of one dollar is made, whether on principal or on interest, the settler gets credit for two dollars.
The Minister has quoted the point of view of Mr. Price. Is Mr. Price the president of the Saskatoon local of the settlers' union, or just what position does he occupy?
He signs himself, president of the soldier settlers' union.

That may be the soldier settlers' union for the district of Saskatoon, but that is only one local of the soldier settlers' union. I understand that there are fifty locals of the soldier settlers' union organized in northern Saskatchewan and elsewhere, and I do not think the point of view of these fifty locals is the same as that presented through the minister by the locals stated. I did not know this matter was coming up today and there is some information I have not at my disposal, but I have a letter here from H. S. Clarke, the secretary of the North Battleford local. He farms a short distance from North Battleford. He met the commissioner and General Ross when they went out west last fall to meet the soldier settlers and conferred at Lloydminster, Saskatoon, North Battleford and other places.
I see that Mr. Price gives his address as Lloydminster.

Then that would be the Lloydminster local he was speaking for. What I want to point out is this, that the North Battleford local, I presume, is working in harmony with all the other locals, and therefore I am wondering at the discrepancy between the point of view presented by the minister and Mr. Clarke's conception of the question. Mr. Clarke says:
Our aim is that the debt be as it stood at the time of revaluation in 1929, and no interest charges be made from that date. Any moneys paid in since to be applied to principal only.
If Mr. Clarke has the right slant on this question, then the statement I made previously is sound, that the department is not going as far as I anticipated to meet the wishes of the soldier settlers, and I am wondering if the limits set by the resolution

Soldier Settlement Act
are going to be strictly adhered to by the minister and his department. I rather hope not. I would like to see the minister and the department take as favourable a view of the whole situation as possible.

I shall reserve most of what I have to say until the bill is before us. Did I understand the minister to say that this remission of interest would be from the standard dates in 1932 onward to 1937, for a period of five years, or just for one year?
The interest is remitted for one year. That refers to the interest accruing under the act during the twelve months immediately preceding the standard date in 1932.
So interest is due on present payments? It is just remitted upon arrears?

It is the interest for the
twelve months that have passed. If those interest charges have been paid, the person paying them gets this credit applied on principal. The hon. member for North Battle-ford will probably remember that when the thirty per cent horizontal reduction was made in May, 1930, just near the end of the spring session-
In the last week of the spring session.
That was the date.

The arrears of interest were spread at that time, and the interest that is being remitted entirely is from the standard date in 1931 to the standard in 1932. That is remitted, washed out, and those who paid are given credit for an amount equal to the payments they made. From that time on anyone who pays a dollar gets credit for two dollars.

I am going to ask the minister, when he introduces the bill, to bring down to the house details showing the total cost of administration of the Soldier Settlement Act from the beginning to date; the total cost to the country of the revaluation of stock and equipment; the total cost of the revaluation of land; and after adding all those together I would ask the minister to tell the house whether he has ever thought of the advisability of giving the land to the settlers who still have a flight equity in it and wiping out the whole settlement scheme once and for all.
I am asking for information, not seeking to delay the minister. Will this resolution, or the bill founded upon it, apply to settlers who, so to speak, have followed up the original settlers?
It does apply to them.

My other question is this:
The resolution contains the expression, "the removal of the lien on the equipment of soldier settlers." Does that mean that the lien will be wiped out or turned on to the land?

The amount of money
secured by the lien will not disappear, but the lien will be removed the same as it was removed some time ago on stock and equipment.
It still adheres to the land?
Yes.

There is one further
question I should like to ask the minister before the bill is brought down. At that time I shall have something more to say. What about the soldier settler who year after year for many years has paid to the board his principal and interest and then, just a limited number of years before his principal and interest is paid, passes out, or goes west? What about the dependents of that man? Will the department modify the legislation in any way so that the property will pass into the hands of the dependents? Because if the money is not paid, and the breadwinner is taken away, they would have to leave their farms and lose all their holdings.
I assume the hon. member is referring to the interests of a deceased soldier settler.
Yes.

As I understand it, the
interest of the deceased in the land devolves upon his dependents and is administered by the estate. Whether or not there are cases where the estate is not able to administer them and suffers hardship, I do not know. There may be such cases.

I think the average
soldier settler is fearful of that condition arising. He feels that if death comes there will be nothing left for those remaining.
Nothing left?

Nothing left, if something is not done to save the estate for those who are left.

Mr.'SPENCER: I believe when the minister was considering bringing down this legislation an opportunity was given to soldier settlers to place their views before him. I should like to ask to what extent the present legislation is in line with their wishes.

The present legislation is not in line with the original view of some of the soldier settlers. A number of them wanted the whole debt wiped out. In fact, I believe some of them asked the return of money they had paid. Of course those differences had to be the subject of conferences, investigations and exchange of views. All the various possibilities of legislation of this type had to be considered. In the main these settlers do not want to be legislated into ownership. The final result was that the legislation drafted as nearly as possible conformed to the views of the majority. I have no doubt in the world there are those who will not be satisfied and, although I am an optimist, I never expected that we could satisfy everybody. I do say however that, in my judgment, as a remedial measure the proposed legislation does deal equitably with the soldier settlers throughout Canada, and others holding contracts with the government. An effort has been made in framing the legislation to see that a penalty is not imposed upon other soldiers, because it must be remembered that soldier settlers represent less than three per cent of the Canadian expeditionary force. There are many soldiers in Canada to-day who are not on land and who are in the same difficulties in which many of us find ourselves. I make the statement, believing it to be true, in the relative sense at any rate, that there are many soldiers who are not in the preferred position that the soldier settler is in, and who have not had the advantage of residing upon lands for the last thirteen or fourteen years. Having that in mind, and also the position of other land owners in the various provinces where different legislative enactments have been passed or are contemplated, the government felt that the best course to follow was to deal with the soldier settlers and others holding lands from coast to coast in the way indicated in the resolution, and which will be set out in greater detail and accuracy in the bill to follow.
I do not believe that the horizontal reduction was at all sound. I cannot help but think it was put through in a hurry, and that at the time consideration was not given to the effect it might have. The effect was not an equitable distribution, I think in so far as it is possible this bill will bring about equitable distribution. Then, again, the government do

not deem it desirable to enter into any such agreements as were entered into with respect to taxes and things of that character. They were not universal or dominion-wide in their application. That was hurriedly done; the so-called agreement was hurriedly entered into. I do not say this in a spirit of ultra-criticism of those who had charge at the time, but in my estimation it was hurriedly done and did not extend to all those under the act the benefit of the so-called agreement. As a matter of fact it applied only to the three western provinces, and was entered into when there was before the then soldier settlement board the opinion of the Department of Justice that it was illegal to do it. I have no doubt it was illegal. I say it was hurriedly entered into in the late spring or early summer of 1930, that it was not a wise procedure to take and has not worked out well. It has given endless trouble; it has taught many settlers to disregard their responsibility to their municipalities, and rendered the position of those municipalities almost hopeless so far as collecting taxes is concerned. Some of the settlers do not consider that municipal taxes are obligations which they should take seriously. I say that with great frankness, because that was one of the results achieved by the so-called tax agreement.

I understand that owing
to poor prices for crops last year the soldier settlers had gTeat difficulty in meeting their one-third crop payment. Is an attempt now being made to collect one-third, or is it being dropped to one-fourth?

In accepting a portion of the crop the director endeavoured to conform to the practice and the law in the various provinces. The provinces would adopt one-third or one-fourth or some other fraction, and the director endeavoured to conform. But the practice now is to accept one-fourth or less, regardless of whether or not the province asked for more.

A lot of these men will have payments coming due for the next ten years, say. The credit of $2 where he has paid $1 applies only for five years. Suppose by some miracle he gets some money-he will not get it out of the land, but his mother-inlaw might die-will he be allowed to pay in advance in order to get this $2 for $1?

year.
